name: Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff Relativistic Star
description: The hydrostatic equilibrium equations for a static, spherically symmetric relativistic star of perfect fluid. They set the maximum mass of neutron stars before collapse to a black hole.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A star is a truce between gravity, which pulls its matter inward, and pressure, which pushes back. Writing that truce down in Newtonian gravity gives the classical equation of stellar structure, and closing it requires one more ingredient: a relation between pressure and density, an equation of state [phillips1999]. The oldest useful choice is a polytrope, $p = K\rho^{\gamma}$, which reduces the whole problem to the Lane-Emden equation studied since the nineteenth century [lane1870]. The Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equation is the version of that truce in general relativity, and a polytrope, or some richer equation of state in its place, turns the equation into a model of a star.¶The relativistic story has a sharp lineage. In 1931 Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar fed a relativistically degenerate electron gas, itself a polytrope, into the Newtonian equations and discovered that white dwarfs possess a maximum mass, above which electron degeneracy pressure cannot hold the star up [chandrasekhar1931]. Lev Landau reached a limit of about 1.5 solar masses independently, in a paper he wrote in Zurich in February 1931 and published the next year, and guessed that heavier stars hold regions where "atomic nuclei come in close contact, forming one gigantic nucleus" [landau1932, yakovlev2013]. Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky went further in 1934, proposing that a supernova marks "the transition of an ordinary star into a neutron star, consisting mainly of neutrons" [baade1934].¶Eight years after Chandrasekhar, Richard Tolman gave a systematic method for static spheres of perfect fluid in full general relativity [tolman1939], and in the immediately following paper J. Robert Oppenheimer and George Volkoff applied the relativistic equilibrium equation to a cold gas of neutrons, deriving what is now called the TOV equation and finding that neutron cores, too, have a maximum mass [oppenheimer1939]. Above three quarters of a solar mass they found no static solution, and concluded that a massive enough star, its nuclear fuel spent, will "contract indefinitely, although more and more slowly, never reaching true equilibrium" [oppenheimer1939]. Their estimate was crude, but the conclusion was momentous: beyond it, nothing known could stop collapse.¶The TOV equation, fed a polytrope, is therefore the workhorse of the physics of compact stars. By itself the equation is underdetermined: it relates pressure, density, and the enclosed mass, but cannot say how pressure responds to compression. Supply that closure, whether an idealized polytrope or a detailed nuclear equation of state, and the TOV equation returns a family of stars with one parameter, a curve of mass against radius, and a maximum mass past which static equilibrium is impossible and a black hole must form. Clifford Rhoades and Remo Ruffini showed in 1974 that causality and general relativity alone cap that maximum for a neutron star at 3.2 solar masses, whatever the equation of state does where it is unknown, which gave observers a way to tell a neutron star from a black hole by weighing it [rhoades1974].¶Neutron stars stayed on paper until 1968, when Antony Hewish, Jocelyn Bell, and three colleagues at the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory in Cambridge reported a radio source pulsing with extreme regularity, which they suggested "may be associated with oscillations of white dwarf or neutron stars" [hewish1968]. Within months Thomas Gold argued that the steady period is the rotation of a neutron star, its radiation sweeping past like "a rotating beacon" [gold1968]. The location of the maximum, near two solar masses for neutron stars, is now among the most pointed questions in physics, probed by pulsar timing, by the X-ray sizing of neutron stars, and by the gravitational waves of merging compact objects, each measurement a constraint on which equation of state the TOV equation should be given.¶Timing the delay of a pulsar's pulses as they pass its companion, Paul Demorest and colleagues weighed PSR J1614-2230 at $1.97 \pm 0.04$ solar masses in 2010, which ruled out almost every proposed equation of state with hyperons or boson condensates [demorest2010]; John Antoniadis and colleagues found $2.01 \pm 0.04$ solar masses for a pulsar in a 2.46 hour orbit about a white dwarf in 2013 [antoniadis2013], and Thankful Cromartie and colleagues about 2.14 for PSR J0740+6620 [cromartie2020]. Two teams modelling the X-rays that the NICER telescope recorded from the hot spots of PSR J0030+0451 each found in 2019 a star of about 1.4 solar masses and a radius of about 13 kilometers [riley2019, miller2019]. The LIGO and Virgo detectors recorded two neutron stars spiralling together on 17 August 2017 [abbott2017], and the tidal distortion of the stars in their last orbits, together with the demand that the equation of state hold up 1.97 solar masses, gave both radii as $11.9 \pm 1.4$ kilometers [abbott2018].

related.text: The vacuum outside the star. Where the pressure reaches zero, $m(r)$ stops growing and the metric continues as Schwarzschild's with $r_s = 2m$.
The star of constant density, whose structure equations integrate by hand. Its central pressure diverges as $R \to \frac{9}{8}r_s$ [schwarzschild1916b, buchdahl1959].
With Hartland Snyder, a few months later, Oppenheimer followed a star too heavy for any equilibrium as it collapses [oppenheimersnyder1939].

coordinates.name: Spherical

parameters.description: Redshift function, dimensionless since it sits in an exponential: a clock held at radius $r$ runs at $e^{\Phi}$ of the rate $t$ counts. It is finite at the centre, and outside the star $e^{2\Phi} = 1 - 2GM/(c^2r)$, which fixes the constant it would otherwise carry

Mass function, a length: $m = GM(r)/c^2$ with $M(r)$ the mass inside the sphere of radius $r$, so $\partial_r m = 4\pi Gr^2\rho/c^2$ and $m(0) = 0$. The chart needs $2m < r$ everywhere, and beyond the surface of the star $m$ is the constant $GM/c^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The redshift function $\Phi(r)$ is dimensionless, and the mass function $m(r)$ is a length, $m = GM(r)/c^2$ with $M(r)$ the mass inside the sphere of radius $r$, and we leave both free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
